visual_evidence: Light-coloured round wooden dowel broken completely into two pieces across the lower-middle of the frame, resting on a wooden bench with metal pins
Long, pointed splinter extending downward along the grain from the left side of the upper piece's break
Matching recessed groove along the grain on the upper-left side of the lower piece where the splinter pulled out
Roughly transverse, slightly jagged break across the remaining right portion of the dowel's cross-section on both pieces
Straight, fine wood grain running parallel to the dowel axis with uniform tan colour and no dark decay streaks or knots visible near the break
diagnosis.probable_cause: A single bending load exceeded the dowel's bending capacity, crushing the fibres on the transverse side in compression and pulling a long splinter along the grain on the opposite tension side.
alternative_modes: A split along the grain leaves the piece separated lengthwise while remaining in one length, whereas this dowel broke completely across the transverse section as well as splintering.

solutions.title: Add an intermediate support
solutions.description: Place a support bracket or block near the middle of the span so the unsupported bending length is cut in half.
pros: Reuses the ~10 mm dowel size with ~1 support block and ~2 fasteners
cons: Requires mounting space at ~120 mm along the span and ~15 min assembly time

span_computed.basis: Idealised beam with the load at mid-span and simple supports at each end, same load and section. Peak bending moment M = F·L/4 grows with the span L, and so does the peak bending stress; deflection δ = F·L³/(48·E·I) grows with the span cubed. Real supports and loads differ, so treat these as ratios, not exact values.

solutions.title: Move the load closer to a support
solutions.description: Reposition the applied load or mating linkage closer to one of the end supports rather than loading the middle of the ~240 mm span.
pros: Uses the existing ~10 mm dowel geometry with no extra parts
cons: Requires relocating mating attachment brackets (~15 min adjustment)

solutions.title: Increase the dowel diameter
solutions.description: Replace the ~10 mm dowel with a larger ~16 mm straight-grained hardwood dowel.
pros: Keeps a single-piece wood rod across the ~240 mm span with ~5 min cut time
cons: Requires drilling out mating holes from ~10 mm to ~16 mm (~5 min) and needs 6 mm more radial clearance

section_computed.basis: Same material, length and load. Weight scales with cross-section area. Bending strength scales with the section modulus (diameter cubed for a round section; width x thickness squared for a rectangle bent across its thickness). Stiffness scales with the second moment of area (diameter to the fourth; width x thickness cubed). These are ratios for the same load, not stress-concentration values: holes, notches and sharp corners are not included.

solutions.title: Switch to an aluminium 6061-T6 rod
solutions.description: Replace the ~10 mm wooden dowel with a ~10 mm diameter aluminium 6061-T6 round rod cut to the same ~240 mm length.
pros: Drop-in fit for existing ~10 mm mounting holes with no frame modifications
cons: Higher material cost than a wooden dowel and ~10 min metal cutting and deburring time

rejected_alternative.visual_feature: Long, pointed splinter extending downward along the grain from the left side of the upper piece's break and matching pulled-out groove on the lower piece
rejected_alternative.reason: A brash failure snaps almost flat across the grain with short splinters or none and typically shows discoloured, soft, or cross-grained wood, whereas this sound dowel pulled a long fibrous splinter along the grain.

diagnosis.mode_source: USDA Forest Products Laboratory, Wood Handbook: Wood as an Engineering Material, FPL-GTR-282 (2021)
diagnosis.summary: The wooden dowel snapped from a single bending overload, pulling a long splinter along the grain on the stretched side.
